displayQuote: Hard times create strong men, strong men create good times, good times create weak men, and weak men create hard times

meta.title: Who really said "Hard times create strong men"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Ibn Khaldun, and not ancient. It is from G. Michael Hopf's post-apocalyptic novel 'Those Who Remain' (2016) — the author has confirmed it himself, and he is still alive and in copyright.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hard times create strong men'?
meta.ogDescription: A 2016 novel, not a 14th-century classic. G. Michael Hopf wrote it; the Ibn Khaldun attribution is baseless, though the underlying cycle really is in the Muqaddimah.

answer.label: Verified — and much newer than people think
answer.authorDates: b. 1971 · American novelist and former US Marine
answer.sourceLine: It is from Those Who Remain (2016), the seventh book in G. Michael Hopf’s post-apocalyptic New World series. Hopf has confirmed the line himself and says he wrote it in 2015, inspired by Strauss–Howe generational theory. It is not ancient, not Arabic, and not a proverb — and because Hopf is alive and writing, it is under copyright worldwide.

source.excerpt: Hard times create strong men. Strong men create good times. Good times create weak men. And, weak men create hard times.
trail: Hopf has published his own account of writing the line while working on book seven of the series, and names Strauss–Howe generational theory as the inspiration. He notes the underlying idea has older roots in Ibn Khaldun and Plato — but does not claim either man wrote the sentence the author’s account ↗.
Note the punctuation in the published text: four separate sentences, with a comma in ‘And, weak men.’ The meme version runs it together as one comma-spliced sentence — the commonest wording variant.
The Ibn Khaldun attribution fails at the source: the sentence does not appear in the Muqaddimah (1377) in any standard translation how the meme spread ↗.

source.rightsNote: In copyright — treat with care. G. Michael Hopf is a living author and Those Who Remain (2016) is protected worldwide for his lifetime plus seventy years. A short quotation with full attribution — author, title, year — is normal quotation practice, but this line is not free stock content: do not put it on merchandise, in advertising, or on a print for sale without permission, and do not describe it as an ancient proverb to sidestep the question. The Ibn Khaldun myth is convenient precisely because it makes a copyrighted sentence look public domain. This is not legal advice.

author.bio: G. Michael Hopf is a bestselling American author of post-apocalyptic and western fiction, and a former US Marine and executive protection agent. His New World series imagines the collapse of society after an electromagnetic pulse. He is the rare living writer to have produced a line so widely repeated that people assume it must be centuries old — and he has spent years politely explaining that he wrote it.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: The authorship is settled — the author is alive and has confirmed it. What keeps this quote in dispute is a persistent effort to age it by six hundred years.

items.why: The sentence appears nowhere in the Muqaddimah (1377) in any standard translation. Historians of the text have said so directly; the citation is always given without a page number, because there is none.

The Muqaddimah describes a four-generation decay of asabiyyah — group feeling: desert hardiness produces conquest, conquest produces luxury, luxury dissolves solidarity, and the dynasty falls. That really is a cycle of hardness and softness. It is not this sentence, and the difference matters.
Also offered as Sallust, Gibbon, or Plato’s Republic Book VIII. None is sourced. Hopf’s own stated inspiration was Strauss–Howe generational theory, a 1990s American framework.
The published text is four full sentences, with a comma in ‘And, weak men create hard times.’ The circulating version compresses it into a single comma-spliced line.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely G. Michael Hopf, Those Who Remain (2016) — a novel published within the last decade, by an author who is alive to confirm it his account ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It offers a complete theory of history in four clauses, and it flatters whoever is quoting it: hard times are coming, and you are the strong one. Its neat circularity is also what makes it feel ancient — proverbs sound like this.

That is exactly why the attribution drifted. A line this tidy invites a distinguished author, and a 14th-century Arab historian lends it the authority of a law of nature rather than a plot beat in an EMP thriller.
context.detailsSummary: Why the Ibn Khaldun credit is so sticky
detailsBody: There is a real cyclical theory in the Muqaddimah — so the claim survives a casual check.
Ibn Khaldun died in 1406, which would make the line public domain and free to sell on posters. Hopf’s copyright makes it neither.
Hopf himself acknowledges the older intellectual lineage, and that gracious remark gets quoted back as though he were conceding authorship.
The saying spikes on social media in hard times, when nobody stops to check a citation that flatters them.
context.pull: The myth is convenient: a 14th-century author would make a copyrighted sentence free.
